name: 3rd Grade Math
blurb: Multiplication and division, properties, addition and subtraction within 1,000, fractions, measurement, data, area, perimeter and shapes.

units.name: Understanding Multiplication
units.blurb: Equal groups, arrays, skip counting by 2s, 5s and 10s, and multiplication word problems.
targets: I can write a multiplication expression for a picture or story of equal groups and tell what each factor means.
I can describe an array with rows and columns and find the total by multiplying.
I can multiply by 2, 5, and 10 using skip counting and patterns.
I can solve equal-group, array, and measurement word problems by drawing a model and writing a multiplication equation.

units.name: Understanding Division
units.blurb: Division as sharing and as grouping, division as an unknown factor, and division word problems.
targets: I can share a total equally among a number of groups and write a division equation for how many are in each group.
I can make groups of a given size from a total and write a division equation for how many groups there are.
I can solve a division fact by finding the missing factor in a related multiplication fact and write fact families.
I can solve sharing and grouping word problems within 100 with a drawing and a division equation.

units.name: Properties and Fact Strategies
units.blurb: Commutative, associative and distributive properties, facts with 0 and 1, and strategies for all facts to 10 × 10.
targets: I can use the commutative property to turn an array or fact around and know the product stays the same.
I can regroup three factors to make multiplying easier and show the product is the same.
I can break a factor into two easier parts, multiply each part, and add the two products.
I can explain and use the rules for multiplying by 0 and 1 and dividing by 1 and by the same number.
I can find any fact to 10 × 10 with a strategy such as doubling, adding a group, or subtracting a group.

units.name: Rounding, Addition, and Subtraction within 1,000
units.blurb: Round to the nearest 10 and 100, add and subtract within 1,000, and estimate to check.
skills: Estimating to Check Sums and Differences
targets: I can round a whole number to the nearest 10 by finding the two tens it is between and deciding which is closer.
I can round a whole number to the nearest 100 by finding the two hundreds it is between and deciding which is closer.
I can add within 1,000 using place value strategies and the standard algorithm, regrouping when needed.
I can subtract within 1,000 using place value strategies and the standard algorithm, including across zeros.
I can round to estimate a sum or difference and decide whether an exact answer is reasonable.

units.name: Unknowns, Patterns, and Two-Step Problems
units.blurb: Missing numbers in equations, unknowns in every position, multiples of 10, table patterns, and two-step problems.
skills: Unknown Numbers in Multiplication and Division Equations
Word Problems with Unknowns in Any Position
Patterns in the Addition and Multiplication Tables
Solving Two-Step Problems and Checking Reasonableness
targets: I can find the missing number in a multiplication or division equation in any position, such as 8 × ? = 48 or 5 = ? ÷ 3.
I can write an equation with a symbol for the unknown when the total, the group size, or the number of groups is missing, and solve it.
I can multiply a one-digit number by a multiple of 10 using place value, such as 4 × 60 = 4 × 6 tens = 24 tens = 240.
I can describe a pattern in an addition or multiplication table and explain it using properties or even and odd numbers.
I can write an equation with a letter for the unknown to represent a two-step word problem.
I can solve two-step word problems with the four operations and use rounding or mental math to check that the answer makes sense.

units.name: Understanding Fractions
units.blurb: Unit fractions, fractions built from unit fractions, and fractions on number lines.
skills: Unit Fractions on a Number Line
targets: I can name the unit fraction 1/b for one of b equal parts of a whole and tell whether parts are equal.
I can explain that a/b is a copies of 1/b and name a fraction shown by a model or a story.
I can partition the interval from 0 to 1 into b equal parts and locate 1/b on a number line.
I can locate a/b on a number line by marking off a lengths of 1/b from 0, including fractions greater than 1.

units.name: Equivalent and Comparing Fractions
units.blurb: Equivalent fractions with models and number lines, whole numbers as fractions, and comparing fractions.
skills: Comparing Fractions with the Same Denominator
Comparing Fractions with the Same Numerator
targets: I can use fraction bars and number lines to show that two fractions are equivalent because they are the same size or the same point.
I can write a simple equivalent fraction (halves, thirds, fourths, sixths, eighths) and explain why it is equivalent with a model.
I can write a whole number as a fraction and recognize fractions such as 6/3 or 4/4 that equal whole numbers.
I can compare two fractions with the same denominator by comparing numerators, record with >, =, <, and justify with a model.
I can compare two fractions with the same numerator by reasoning about the size of the pieces and justify with a model.

units.name: Time, Liquid Volume, and Mass
units.blurb: Telling time to the minute, elapsed time, and measuring and solving problems with liters, grams, and kilograms.
skills: Telling Time to the Nearest Minute
Measuring Mass in Grams and Kilograms
Liquid Volume and Mass Word Problems
targets: I can read and write time to the nearest minute on an analog clock and a digital clock.
I can find a start time, end time, or elapsed time in minutes using a number line or a clock.
I can read a liquid volume on a scaled container and estimate liquid volumes in liters.
I can read a mass on a scale, choose grams or kilograms, and estimate the mass of everyday objects.
I can add, subtract, multiply, or divide to solve one-step word problems with masses or liquid volumes in the same units.

units.name: Graphs, Measurement Data, and Line Plots
units.blurb: Scaled picture graphs and bar graphs, measuring to the nearest half and fourth inch, and line plots.
skills: Making Scaled Picture Graphs and Bar Graphs
Measuring to the Nearest Half and Quarter Inch
targets: I can use the key of a scaled picture graph, including half symbols, to find and compare amounts.
I can read a scaled bar graph, including bars that end between grid lines, and solve one- and two-step how many more and how many less problems.
I can choose a scale and draw a scaled picture graph or bar graph that matches a data table.
I can measure lengths to the nearest half inch and quarter inch with a ruler.
I can make a line plot of measurement data marked in whole numbers, halves, or fourths and answer questions about it.

units.name: Area
units.blurb: Unit squares, counting square units, area of rectangles, the distributive property, and rectilinear figures.
skills: Measuring Area by Counting Unit Squares
Area of Rectangles: Tile and Multiply
targets: I can explain that area is the number of unit squares that cover a shape with no gaps or overlaps.
I can find area by counting unit squares and name it in square centimeters, square meters, square inches, square feet, or square units.
I can find the area of a rectangle by tiling and show that multiplying the side lengths gives the same area.
I can split a rectangle with side lengths a and b + c into two rectangles and show that its area is a × b + a × c.
I can find the area of a rectilinear figure by splitting it into rectangles that do not overlap and adding their areas.

units.name: Perimeter and Shapes
units.blurb: Perimeter, unknown side lengths, same perimeter or same area, quadrilaterals, and equal-area parts.
targets: I can find the perimeter of a polygon by adding all of its side lengths, including sides that are not labeled.
I can find an unknown side length when I know the perimeter and the other side lengths.
I can draw and compare rectangles that have the same perimeter and different areas, or the same area and different perimeters.
I can sort shapes by their attributes and explain that rhombuses, rectangles, and squares are all quadrilaterals.
I can partition a shape into parts with equal area and name the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole.

standards.3.OA.A.1: Interpret products of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 5 × 7 as the total number of objects in 5 groups of 7 objects each.
standards.3.OA.A.2: Interpret whole-number quotients of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share when 56 objects are partitioned equally into 8 shares, or as a number of shares when 56 objects are partitioned into equal shares of 8 objects each.
standards.3.OA.A.3: Use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems in situations involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number.
standards.3.OA.A.4: Determine the unknown whole number in a multiplication or division equation relating three whole numbers.
standards.3.OA.B.5: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide.
standards.3.OA.B.6: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem.
standards.3.OA.C.7: Fluently multiply and divide within 100, using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division or properties of operations. By the end of Grade 3, know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers.
standards.3.OA.D.8: Solve two-step word problems using the four operations. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
standards.3.OA.D.9: Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table), and explain them using properties of operations.
standards.3.NBT.A.1: Use place value understanding to round whole numbers to the nearest 10 or 100.
standards.3.NBT.A.2: Fluently add and subtract within 1000 using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction.
standards.3.NBT.A.3: Multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10 in the range 10–90 using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.
standards.3.NF.A.1: Understand a fraction 1/b as the quantity formed by 1 part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts; understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b.
standards.3.NF.A.2.a: Represent a fraction 1/b on a number line diagram by defining the interval from 0 to 1 as the whole and partitioning it into b equal parts.
standards.3.NF.A.2.b: Represent a fraction a/b on a number line diagram by marking off a lengths 1/b from 0.
standards.3.NF.A.3.a: Understand two fractions as equivalent (equal) if they are the same size, or the same point on a number line.
standards.3.NF.A.3.b: Recognize and generate simple equivalent fractions, e.g., 1/2 = 2/4, 4/6 = 2/3. Explain why the fractions are equivalent, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.
standards.3.NF.A.3.c: Express whole numbers as fractions, and recognize fractions that are equivalent to whole numbers.
standards.3.NF.A.3.d: Compare two fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator by reasoning about their size; comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole; record with >, =, or < and justify.
standards.3.MD.A.1: Tell and write time to the nearest minute and measure time intervals in minutes. Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of time intervals in minutes.
standards.3.MD.A.2: Measure and estimate liquid volumes and masses of objects using grams, kilograms, and liters. Add, subtract, multiply, or divide to solve one-step word problems involving masses or volumes given in the same units.
standards.3.MD.B.3: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step “how many more” and “how many less” problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs.
standards.3.MD.B.4: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths using rulers marked with halves and fourths of an inch. Show the data by making a line plot marked off in whole numbers, halves, or quarters.
standards.3.MD.C.5.a: A square with side length 1 unit, called a unit square, is said to have one square unit of area, and can be used to measure area.
standards.3.MD.C.5.b: A plane figure which can be covered without gaps or overlaps by n unit squares is said to have an area of n square units.
standards.3.MD.C.6: Measure areas by counting unit squares (square cm, square m, square in, square ft, and improvised units).
standards.3.MD.C.7.a: Find the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths by tiling it, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths.
standards.3.MD.C.7.b: Multiply side lengths to find areas of rectangles with whole-number side lengths in real world and mathematical problems, and represent whole-number products as rectangular areas.
standards.3.MD.C.7.c: Use tiling to show in a concrete case that the area of a rectangle with side lengths a and b + c is the sum of a × b and a × c. Use area models to represent the distributive property.
standards.3.MD.C.7.d: Recognize area as additive. Find areas of rectilinear figures by decomposing them into non-overlapping rectangles and adding the areas of the parts.
standards.3.MD.D.8: Solve problems involving perimeters of polygons, including finding the perimeter given the side lengths, finding an unknown side length, and exhibiting rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas or with the same area and different perimeters.
standards.3.G.A.1: Understand that shapes in different categories may share attributes, and that shared attributes can define a larger category. Recognize rhombuses, rectangles, and squares as examples of quadrilaterals, and draw quadrilaterals that do not belong to any of these subcategories.
standards.3.G.A.2: Partition shapes into parts with equal areas. Express the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole.
